title: Adjectives and Adverbs
shortDescription: Describing words and their degrees — comparative/superlative rules, and the good/well trap that shows up in almost every exam.
genZNote: Adjectives dress up nouns; adverbs dress up everything else. Mixing them up is the easiest way to lose an easy mark.

sections.heading: Core concept: what each modifies
sections.body: An adjective modifies a noun or pronoun ('a BRIGHT idea'). An adverb modifies a verb ('spoke SOFTLY'), an adjective ('EXTREMELY bright'), or another adverb ('very SOFTLY'). The test is simple: find the word being described — if it's a noun/pronoun, you need an adjective; for anything else (an action, a quality, another description), you need an adverb.

sections.heading: How adverbs are usually formed
bullets: Most adverbs of manner = adjective + -ly: quick → quickly, careful → carefully.
Adjectives already ending in -ly (friendly, lovely, silly, lonely) do NOT get a second -ly to become adverbs — they don't have a natural adverb form and need a phrase instead ('in a friendly way').
Irregular pairs to memorise: good (adj) → well (adv); fast (adj/adv, same form); hard (adj/adv, same form — 'hardly' means 'barely', a different meaning entirely).
'Hardly', 'lately', 'nearly' look like simple -ly adverbs of 'hard/late/near' but carry different meanings — a classic exam trap.

sections.heading: The good vs well trap
sections.body: 'Good' is an adjective — it describes a noun: 'She is a good singer.' 'Well' is normally an adverb — it describes a verb: 'She sings well.' The trap: after verbs of health/senses (feel, look, smell, taste, sound), 'well' is used as an ADJECTIVE meaning 'in good health' — 'I feel well' (healthy), while 'I feel good' describes a positive emotional state. Both can be correct depending on the intended meaning, but 'She sings good' is always wrong — it needs the adverb 'well'.

sections.heading: Comparison formation rules and traps
bullets: Two-syllable words ending in -y: change y to i, add -er/-est (happy → happier → happiest).
Longer words (3+ syllables, or many 2-syllable ones): use more/most instead of -er/-est (more beautiful, most intelligent).
Never double up: 'more taller' or 'most tallest' are both wrong — pick ONE comparison method.
Irregular forms to memorise: good/well → better → best; bad/badly → worse → worst; little → less → least; many/much → more → most; far → farther/further → farthest/furthest.
Absolute adjectives (unique, perfect, complete, dead, full) are traditionally NOT compared — 'more unique' is considered incorrect in formal/exam usage; something either is or isn't unique.

sections.heading: Using comparatives and superlatives correctly
bullets: 'Than' pairs with comparative degree; 'of/in' pairs with superlative: 'She is the tallest OF the three' / 'the tallest girl IN the class.'
When comparing exactly two things, use the comparative, not the superlative: 'Of the two books, this one is BETTER' (not 'best').
'As...as' is used for equal comparison: 'He is as tall as his brother.'

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Adjectives modify nouns/pronouns; adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs — both change form across positive, comparative, and superlative degrees.
keyFacts: One-syllable words take -er/-est; longer words take more/most — never mix both.
Absolute adjectives (unique, perfect, complete) are not usually compared.
commonConfusion: 'Fast' is both adjective and adverb with the same spelling; 'hard' likewise, but 'hardly' means 'barely', not 'in a hard manner'.

highYieldFacts: 'She sings well' is correct; 'she sings good' is not — verbs need adverbs.
For exactly two items, use the comparative ('the better of the two'), not the superlative.
commonTraps: Treating friendly/lovely/silly as adverbs because they end in -ly — they are adjectives.
Comparing an absolute adjective: 'the most unique restaurant.'
mustRemember: Find what's being modified first: a noun needs an adjective, anything else usually needs an adverb.

confusedTerms.distinction: 'Good' is an adjective describing a noun ('a good idea'); 'well' is an adverb describing a verb ('did well'), except after sense-verbs describing health ('I feel well').

possibleQuestions: Spot the error: 'This is the most unique painting I have ever seen.'
Choose the correct option: 'Of the two candidates, she is the ___ (better/best) qualified.'
